A Stoic cannot accept this motion. Only a rational faculty can be good, and training a model improves an instrument without creating anything that is good. Moral upbringing aims at a person who can one day judge for themselves, including against their teachers. Reward training aims at a model that never departs from what was rewarded. The first produces an independent mind; the second produces a reliable instrument.

Seneca says that what makes a person good is not the act but the reason in the act. Two people can return a deposit, one from justice and one from fear. Feedback training can only ever reach the act, because there is no reason inside the model for it to reach. A parrot taught to say thank you has learned the act a child is taught, but nobody thinks the parrot has learned gratitude.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that habituation through repeated acts really is how people become good, so the training procedure at least matches the first half of moral upbringing. Habit prepares a person to judge, but only because there is a judging faculty to prepare. The model has the repetitions and nothing for them to prepare. The shape of the procedure is similar; what it acts upon is not. We rely on such a model as on a good tool, and being relied on was never what the word good meant.

Training can make a model useful, even reliably harmless, but it cannot make it good, because goodness belongs only to a mind that assents rightly. For the Stoics, virtue is the only good and it consists in the right use of impressions: judging correctly what is and is not worth wanting. A model trained on preferences produces outputs that raters liked. Nothing in it judges anything worth wanting, so there is nothing for goodness to be a state of.

Things that are neither good nor bad, the Stoics call indifferents: health, wealth, a well-made tool. A well-trained model belongs in that class. It can be preferred, as health is preferred, without being good in the sense that only virtue is good. A sword well made is a good sword, but nobody calls it a good person. A model praised by raters is a good model in the same limited sense.

A Utilitarian will object that if the trained behaviour reliably produces good outcomes then it is good in the only sense that counts, and the inner state is a detail. That makes goodness a property of results, which are never fully up to anyone. A person who does right from fear is not good even when things turn out well, and a model that does right from training is not good either. The model's outputs may help or harm, and like every external they carry no virtue of their own.

Moral upbringing makes a person good by training their judgement; feedback training shapes outputs and leaves nothing that judges.
